Fractional CFO South Africa

Senior financial leadership.
Without the full time cost.

A fractional CFO gives you financial strategy, clarity and decision support without the cost of a full time executive.

What is a fractional CFO

A CFO for your business.
Not your payroll.

A fractional CFO is a senior finance professional who works with your business on a part time basis. You get strategic thinking, financial modelling, cash flow management and decision support at a fraction of a full time cost.

A fractional arrangement gives you senior finance expertise at a fixed monthly fee, scaled to what your business actually needs.

The difference

Full time CFO

R1.2m to R2m per year. One person. Full time overhead. Often too expensive until you reach significant scale.

Bookkeeper or accountant

Records what happened. Does not tell you what it means or what to do next. Essential, but not enough on its own.

Fractional CFO

Senior finance leadership on a retained basis. Strategy, modelling, cash flow, funding and decision support at a price that works for your stage.

Common questions

Fractional CFO FAQ

How is a fractional CFO different from my accountant?

Your accountant handles compliance. A fractional CFO focuses on financial strategy, cash flow, modelling and the decisions that drive growth. The two roles complement each other.

How many hours per month do I need?

It depends on your business complexity and needs. Some businesses need 8 hours per month for reporting and a monthly strategy session. Others need 20 to 30 hours for active modelling or fundraising. We agree a fixed scope upfront.

Can I start with bookkeeping and add CFO support later?

Yes. Most clients start with monthly bookkeeping and add fractional CFO services as their business grows. There is no obligation to take both from day one.

How quickly can we get started?

After an initial consultation we can typically have a scope and engagement letter to you within 48 hours, and be operational within one week.

Funding Readiness South Africa

Get your business
funding-ready.

Whether you are approaching a bank, investor or alternative lender, your financial information needs to be accurate, current and professionally presented.

Why it matters

Most businesses lose funding
before they even apply.

Banks and investors do not just evaluate your idea. They evaluate your numbers. Incomplete financials, inconsistent forecasts and poorly structured funding requests are the most common reasons businesses fail to secure finance.

Funding readiness means having accurate historical financials, a credible forward looking model and a clear, professional presentation of what you need and how it will be used.

What lenders look for

At least 24 months of clean, reconciled management accounts. A credible cash flow forecast. A clear view of how the money will be used and repaid.

What investors look for

A financial model with clear assumptions, scenario analysis and a returns framework. Evidence that the team understands the numbers driving the business.

What alternative lenders look for

Consistent revenue, manageable debt levels, positive cash flow trends and a realistic repayment plan based on actual trading history.

What we prepare

Everything you need
to secure funding.

02

04

06

Bookkeeping 5 min read

5 Signs Your Business Books Are Not in Good Shape

You do not need to be an accountant to know when your books are not working properly. Here are five warning signs.

Good bookkeeping is not about having perfect spreadsheets. It is about having reliable financial information when you need it. Your books should give you confidence in your numbers, not create more questions.

1. You do not trust your numbers

If you regularly question whether your profit, cash balance or expenses are accurate, your books need attention. Business owners should be able to look at their management accounts and trust what they see. If you find yourself second-guessing the figures or unsure whether they reflect reality, that is a sign something has gone wrong in the recording process.

Inaccurate books do not just create uncertainty. They lead to poor decisions made on the basis of information that does not reflect what is actually happening in the business.

2. Bank reconciliations are months behind

Your accounting records should regularly agree to your actual bank accounts. If they do not, errors can easily build up. Unreconciled accounts mean transactions may be missing, duplicated or incorrectly categorised.

A well-run set of books is reconciled monthly at minimum. If your last reconciliation was three months ago, the gap between your records and reality is likely larger than you think.

3. You only look at your numbers at year-end

Waiting for your accountant to tell you how the business performed means you are making decisions without current financial information. By the time the annual accounts are ready, the information is often six to twelve months old.

Monthly management accounts give you a current picture of revenue, expenses, profit and cash. Without them, you are running the business without visibility.

4. Your debtors and creditors are not accurate

If you do not know who owes you money or what you owe suppliers, your cash flow can quickly become difficult to manage. Debtor and creditor balances that are not kept current lead to missed collections, late payments and an inaccurate picture of what cash the business actually has available.

An accurate debtors ledger tells you who to chase. An accurate creditors ledger tells you what is due and when. Both are essential for managing cash effectively.

5. Your bookkeeping is always playing catch-up

If invoices, expenses and transactions are constantly being processed weeks or months later, your accounts are not giving you a current view of the business. Bookkeeping that is perpetually behind is not just inefficient. It creates a backlog that compounds over time and makes it harder to produce accurate reports when you need them.

Reliable books are maintained regularly, not in one large batch at quarter-end when someone finally has time.

If any of these sound familiar

Fractional CFO 4 min read

Why Your Business May Need a Fractional CFO

You do not always need a full time CFO. But as your business grows, you may need someone who can look beyond the bookkeeping and help you understand what the numbers actually mean.

A Fractional CFO gives you access to senior finance expertise without the cost of hiring a full time CFO. The right level of financial expertise, when you need it.

As a business grows, the financial decisions become more complex. Revenue increases, costs multiply, funding becomes a possibility and the numbers start to matter more than they used to. A bookkeeper keeps your records accurate and up to date. But there comes a point where accurate records are not enough on their own.

That is where a Fractional CFO can make a significant difference.

What a Fractional CFO can help with

A Fractional CFO works with your business on a part time or retained basis. They look at the numbers your bookkeeper produces and help you understand what they mean and what to do with them.

  • Cash flow forecasting and planning
  • Budgets and financial models
  • Understanding profitability and margins
  • Funding and lender requirements
  • Management reporting and board packs
  • Scenario planning before making major decisions
  • Improving financial controls and processes
  • Helping you understand where your business is heading

The difference between a bookkeeper and a Fractional CFO

Your bookkeeper keeps your financial records accurate and up to date. A Fractional CFO takes those numbers and helps turn them into better financial decisions.

Think of it this way. A bookkeeper tells you what happened. A Fractional CFO tells you what it means and what to do about it.

Bookkeeper

Records transactions, reconciles accounts, keeps books tidy. Tells you what happened.

Fractional CFO

Interprets the numbers, builds strategy, supports decisions. Tells you what to do next.

When does it make sense?

Fractional CFO support can be particularly valuable when your business is growing quickly, considering funding, preparing for an acquisition, expanding into new markets, or finding that financial decisions are becoming more complex.

You do not need a CFO sitting in your office every day. You need the right level of financial expertise when you need it. That is where a Fractional CFO makes sense.

Funding Readiness 4 min read

Funding Readiness: Are You Ready to Raise Finance?

Getting funding is not just about finding a lender. It is about being ready when the lender starts asking questions.

What lenders need

Up to date accounts, cash flow forecasts, clear funding purpose

What slows it down

Outdated records, unclear cash flow, inconsistent management information

The right time to prepare

Before you need the funding, not when you are already under pressure

The outcome

A faster process, clearer lender picture, better options available

The best time to prepare for funding is before you need it. Businesses that approach lenders with complete, well-organised financial information are in a much stronger position than those that start preparing after the conversation has already begun.

Many businesses approach lenders with a funding requirement but are not prepared for the level of detail required. Outdated accounts, unclear cash flow, inconsistent management information or a poorly explained funding request can slow the process down or reduce the options available.

What funding readiness actually means

Funding readiness means having the right information in place before you approach the market. This typically includes:

  • Up to date financial statements
  • Management accounts that reflect the current state of the business
  • Cash flow forecasts with clear, realistic assumptions
  • A clear understanding of your existing debt
  • A realistic view of how much the business can afford to borrow

The questions every lender will ask

Just as importantly, you need to be able to clearly explain what the funding is for, how much you need, and how the business will repay it. Lenders are not just evaluating your numbers. They are evaluating whether you understand your own business well enough to manage borrowed capital responsibly.

A well-prepared funding pack can make the process more efficient and give lenders a clearer picture of the business. It also demonstrates that the management team has thought carefully about the decision.

What funding readiness applies to

Whether you are funding growth, purchasing equipment, managing working capital or refinancing existing debt, preparation matters. The funding purpose does not change the need for accurate, current financial information.

Growth funding

Expanding operations, hiring, entering new markets

Asset finance

Purchasing equipment, vehicles or property

Working capital

Managing cash flow gaps or seasonal funding needs

Refinancing

Restructuring existing debt on better terms

Prepare before you need it

The best time to prepare for funding is before you need it. Businesses that start the process with clean books, current management accounts and a clear funding narrative are in a significantly stronger position than those that begin preparing under time pressure.

If funding is something you are considering in the next six to twelve months, the time to start getting your financial information in order is now.
